blocks.html: You may have wondered why it needs the name :foo. This name is important because it signifies that this live loop is different from all other live loops.
There can never be two live loops running with the same name.
This means that if we want multiple concurrently running live loops, we just need to give them different names:

blocks.source:
live_loop :foo do
  use_synth :prophet
  play :c1, release: 8, cutoff: rrand(70, 130)
  sleep 8
end

live_loop :bar do
  sample :bd_haus
  sleep 0.5
end

blocks.html: You can now update and change each live loop independently and it all just works.

One thing you might have already noticed is that live loops work automatically with the thread cue mechanism we explored previously. Every time the live loop loops, it generates a new cue event with the name of the live loop. We can therefore sync on these cues to ensure our loops are in sync without having to stop anything.

blocks.source:
live_loop :foo do
  play :e4, release: 0.5
  sleep 0.4
end

live_loop :bar do
  sample :bd_haus
  sleep 1
end

blocks.html: Let’s see if we can fix the timing and sync without stopping it. First, let’s fix the :foo loop to make the sleep a factor of 1 - something like 0.5 will do:

blocks.source:
live_loop :foo do
  play :e4, release: 0.5
  sleep 0.5
end

live_loop :bar do
  sample :bd_haus
  sleep 1
end

blocks.html: We’re not quite finished yet though - you’ll notice that the beats don’t quite line up correctly. This is because the loops are out of phase. Let’s fix that by syncing one to the other:

blocks.source:
live_loop :foo do
  play :e4, release: 0.5
  sleep 0.5
end

live_loop :bar do
  sync :foo
  sample :bd_haus
  sleep 1
end

blocks.html: Wow, everything is now perfectly in time - all without stopping.
Now, go forth and live code with live loops!
